title: Paraphrasing What You Hear
keyIdea: To paraphrase something you heard, you say it again in your own words and keep the meaning exactly the same. Start with the main idea, then the key details, in the order you heard them. Swap words for ones that mean the same, and watch for swaps that change the facts: most is not all, rarely is not never, about is not exactly. Repeating the same words is copying, and adding or changing a fact is not a paraphrase.
familyTip: Read your child a short paragraph from a news story or a non-fiction book, once, with the book closed to them. Ask them to tell it back in their own words. Then read it again together and check: did any fact change (a number, who did it, some or all)?

visual.caption: You heard: Most owls hunt at night and sleep during the day. Drag each retelling, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Most owls hunt at night and sleep during the day.
Most owls rest by day and look for food after dark.
At night most owls hunt; by day they sleep.
Most owls hunt by day and sleep at night.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort copy, paraphrase or changed meaning, find the main idea, swap words safely, spot a changed fact, retell in order.

kid: To paraphrase means to say what you heard in your own words. The meaning must stay the same. Bees go to flowers for nectar is a paraphrase of Bees visit flowers to collect nectar.
First think: what was the whole talk about? That is the main idea. Say that first. Then add the key details in the order you heard them.
Swap words for ones that mean the same. Careful! Some swaps change the facts. Most owls is not all owls. Rarely is not never. About 50 is not exactly 50.
Saying the very same words is copying, not paraphrasing. Adding a fact you did not hear is not a paraphrase either. Check who did it, what happened, how many and when.
adult: Ages 9 to 10. The US Common Core asks Grade 4 pupils to paraphrase parts of a text read aloud or shown in other media (SL.4.2). Grade 5 pupils summarise them (SL.5.2). In England, the spoken language strand asks pupils to listen and respond and to give clear answers. From Year 3, reading asks them to find main ideas across paragraphs and sum them up.

Paraphrasing a heard text is harder than paraphrasing a written one, because the listener cannot look back. A good routine: hold on to the main idea first, then two or three key details in the order they came, then put each into new words. Changing the word order or grammar is fine. Changing a quantifier (most to all), a number (400 to 40), a degree (rarely to never) or who did what is not.

Common mistakes: repeating the speaker word for word and calling it a paraphrase; picking a vivid small detail instead of the main idea; adding facts or opinions that were never said; swapping in a stronger or weaker word, such as never for rarely or exactly for about; and mixing up who did what when the sentence is turned round. A paraphrase is not always shorter; a summary is the shorter cousin.

In the lab your child sorts six retellings into copied, paraphrase or meaning changed and picks the main idea of three short talks. They drag in safe word swaps for five sentences, tap the word that changed a fact in five retellings, and retell three short talks in order. A Hear it button reads each one aloud where the browser can speak.

practice.prompt: You heard: "Penguins cannot fly, but they swim very fast." Which is a paraphrase?
choices: Penguins are speedy swimmers, though they can't fly.
Penguins cannot fly, but they swim very fast.
Penguins can fly and swim fast.
practice.hint: New words, same meaning. Check every fact.
practice.explain: Speedy swimmers and can't fly keep both facts. The second is a copy; the third changes a fact.

practice.prompt: A talk had {k} key points. Lily's retelling kept {j} of them. How many key points did she miss?
practice.hint: Take the points she kept away from all the points in the talk.
practice.explain: {k} − {j} = {=k-j} key points were missed. A good paraphrase keeps every key point.

practice.prompt: "The museum is closed on Mondays." Which retelling changes the meaning?
choices: The museum is shut every day.
On Mondays the museum is shut.
You can't visit the museum on a Monday.
practice.hint: Check when: which one changes the day?
practice.explain: every day changes when it is closed. The other two keep the meaning in new words.

practice.prompt: A talk lasted {m} minutes. Ana's retelling of it took {r} minutes. How many minutes shorter was her retelling?
practice.hint: Take the length of the retelling away from the length of the talk.
practice.explain: {m} − {r} = {=m-r} minutes shorter. A retelling can be shorter as long as the main idea and key facts stay the same.

practice.prompt: "Lucy rarely watches TV." Which swap keeps the meaning?
choices: Lucy hardly ever watches TV.
Lucy never watches TV.
Lucy often watches TV.
practice.hint: Rarely means sometimes, but not often.
practice.explain: hardly ever means the same as rarely. never is stronger and often is the opposite.

pool.prompt: What does it mean to paraphrase?
choices: Say it in your own words with the same meaning.
Say the same words again.
Add your own facts to it.
pool.hint: Think about whose words you use, and what happens to the meaning.
pool.explain: A paraphrase uses your own words and keeps the meaning. Repeating is copying; adding facts changes it.

pool.prompt: A talk is about how frogs grow from eggs to adults. What is the main idea?
choices: Frogs change a lot as they grow.
Frogs have long tongues.
Frogs are green.
pool.hint: What is every part of the talk about?
pool.explain: The whole talk is about how frogs grow and change. The others are details or were not said.

pool.prompt: Zoe heard {a} short talks on Monday and {b} on Tuesday. She paraphrased each one once. How many paraphrases did she give?
pool.hint: Add the talks from both days.
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} paraphrases, one for each talk she heard.

pool.prompt: You heard: "Some birds fly south in winter." Which retelling has a slip?
choices: Every bird flies south in winter.
In winter, some birds head south.
A number of birds fly south when it is winter.
pool.hint: Look for a word like some, all or every.
pool.explain: Every changes some to all, so the meaning changed.

pool.prompt: You heard: "Ben thanked the driver." Which is a fair paraphrase?
choices: Ben said thank you to the driver.
The driver thanked Ben.
Ben shouted at the driver.
pool.hint: Who did the thanking, and who was thanked?
pool.explain: Ben said thank you keeps who did what. The second swaps them; the third changes the action.

pool.prompt: Mo retold {t} short talks. {c} of them changed a fact. How many were fair paraphrases?
pool.hint: Take away the ones that changed a fact.
pool.explain: {t} − {c} = {=t-c} were fair paraphrases. Any changed fact means it is not a paraphrase.

pool.prompt: "The trip was cancelled." Which word can replace cancelled?
choices: called off
delayed
planned
pool.hint: Did the trip happen at all?
pool.explain: called off means it did not happen, like cancelled. delayed means it happened later.

pool.prompt: Why is it hard to paraphrase something you hear?
choices: You can't look back at the words.
The words are always longer.
You must use the same words.
pool.explain: When you listen, the words are gone once they are said, so you hold the main idea in your head.

pool.prompt: You heard: "The cake took about an hour to bake." Which swap is fair?
choices: roughly an hour
exactly an hour
over an hour
pool.explain: roughly means about. exactly and over change the meaning.
